recentItems.title: Tracking Health Security Progress and Building Resilience in Africa
recentItems.description:
The world is shifting from a period of urgent health action to one of growing neglect, even as biological threats continue to rise. Against this backdrop, the 2026 Africa Health Security (AHS) Index shows significant progress has been made across the continent – but substantial gaps remain.

In this event, the Brown University Pandemic Center, Economist Enterprise, and the Science for Africa Foundation discuss the findings and recommendations of the 2026 AHS Index, an independent assessment of health security capacities in Africa.

This webinar convened global experts and policymakers to discuss how the AHS Index can shape policy decision-making and drive action to strengthen health security capacities and improve preparedness for future epidemics and pandemics.

recentItems.title: TV Can Save the World, Again
recentItems.description: Nuclear-themed TV shows draw audiences in. From The Day After to today’s shows like Fallout, The Diplomat, and Paradise are adding storylines that remind us of the dangers of the most destructive weapons ever invented. Nuclear risks are rising, and TV can turn the tide again.

recentItems.title: Iran’s Nuclear Future: Implications of the 2026 War
recentItems.description:
The U.S. and Israeli military campaign against Iran may not be focused on Iran’s nuclear program, but critical nuclear questions still loom large. What will happen to Iran’s highly enriched uranium if the regime collapses? Could the war prompt Iran’s new hardline leadership to pursue nuclear weapons? Is a nuclear deal even possible anymore—and if so, how could it ensure that Iran does not go nuclear?

This discussion covers how the war is shaping nuclear security and proliferation risks in Iran and beyond and what can be done to mitigate them.

recentItems.title: AIxBio: A Framework for Managed Access
recentItems.description:
The convergence of AI and the life sciences has driven the development of biological AI tools with a range of beneficial applications. However, some of these tools have also raised concerns among biosecurity experts that they could be misused by malicious actors to cause harm, including by making it easier to engineer dangerous pathogens.

NTI | bio’s paper, A Framework for Managed Access to Biological AI Tools, proposes a managed access approach—allowing only validated users to access tools that contribute to biosecurity risks—a key path towards reducing the risk that such tools will be deliberately misused to cause harm. The paper offers recommendations for funders, model developers, and hosting services to support implementation of managed access.

Informed by interviews with more than 20 experts in biosecurity, biological AI tool development, and bioscience research, the framework adopts two central principles:

1) Access should be tiered based on the tool’s risk level. 
2) The need for security should be balanced with the need to provide equitable access. 

The framework seeks to reduce the risk of misuse without limiting the incredible potential of these tools to benefit humanity.

This virtual event presents an overview of the framework and its potential impact on the risk landscape, discuss how it could be adopted by the scientific community, and how managed access is fundamental for enabling other forms of built-in guardrails.

recentItems.title: Integrating Biosafety & Biosecurity into Funding Decisions
recentItems.description:
Funders play a key role in shaping how life science research is conducted. This webinar will introduce a new framework—developed collaboratively by a diverse group of internationally recognized experts—to help funders identify proposals that may require additional biosafety or biosecurity review and to support appropriate risk-mitigation efforts.

The framework outlines a three-step process:

1.  Rapid Screening to determine whether proposals present elevated biosafety or biosecurity risk

2.  Detailed Assessment for proposals that may involve agents or methods capable of causing large-scale harm if misused or accidentally released

3.  Risk Mitigation to ensure that any identified biosafety or biosecurity risks are addressed through feasible mitigation measures.

The International Bio Funders’ Compact is a public commitment by funders to incorporate biosecurity into decision-making, including pre-award reviews. This framework supports that aim by helping distinguish low-risk projects from those requiring deeper assessment and by recommending practical pathways to proceed safely and securely.

The discussion walks through the core assessment questions to gauge probability and magnitude of harm, considerations for weighing risks and benefits, and practical measures for biosafety, biosecurity, and information management.

recentItems.title: Report Launch: Safeguarding AIxBio Capabilities to Prevent Global Catastrophe
recentItems.description:
With rapidly advancing capabilities at the intersection of AI and biotechnology, the world faces both remarkable opportunities and unprecedented risks.

In February 2025, NTI and the Munich Security Conference (MSC) hosted a tabletop exercise to discuss the opportunities and risks associated with advances in AIxBio capabilities, and to explore innovative approaches for preventing their misuse. The exercise convened high-level international experts in artificial intelligence, biotechnology, international security, and public health to address these critical international security issues.

NTI’s new report, Safeguarding Against Global Catastrophe: Risks, Opportunities, and Governance Options at the Intersection of Artificial Intelligence and Biology, highlights key findings from the discussion and offers recommendations for actions the international community can take to reduce these risks.

The exercise was the fifth collaboration between NTI and MSC and was built around a fictional scenario involving a global pandemic, sparked by a novel virus that was intentionally engineered by an extremist group using artificial intelligence. Exercise participants discussed opportunities to reduce risks while also tapping AI’s potential to improve biosecurity and pandemic preparedness.

Join Brian Tse; James Diggans, PhD; Elizabeth Cameron, PhD; and NTI | bio’s Jaime Yassif, PhD; and Hayley Severance for an interactive panel discussion about the exercise and report.

recentItems.title: A Bipartisan Blueprint for Preventing the Spread of Nuclear Weapons
recentItems.description: The 2025 NTI Board of Directors Dinner featured a discussion with Stephen J. Hadley, Former U.S. National Security Advisor, and Ernest J. Moniz, NTI Co-Chair and CEO, on the findings and recommendations of a new report from the Task Force on Nuclear Proliferation and U.S. National Security, which was initiated by Harvard University’s Belfer Center, the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, and the Nuclear Threat Initiative. The conversation was moderated by former journalist Jeanne Meserve.

recentItems.title: From Adoption to Action: Data-Driven Solutions for Implementing the Pandemic Agreement
recentItems.description:
The world’s first Pandemic Agreement, adopted by the World Health Assembly in May, is a historic step toward building resilient systems to prevent, detect, and respond to epidemic and pandemic threats and save millions of lives. At the same time, many countries—particularly low- and middle-income nations—face significant political and technical hurdles in ratifying and implementing the agreement. 

This webinar explores practical strategies and opportunities for nations to close critical data and preparedness gaps, including by using tools such as the Global Health Security Index and the Africa Health Security Index to guide efforts to build stronger global health security and a world safer from future biological threats.

Join hosts NTI, Brown University Pandemic Center, Economist Impact, and Science for Africa Foundation for this important discussion.

recentItems.title: FutureSafe Innovation Forum: A Conversation with Livermore Director Kimberly S. Budil
recentItems.description:
Join NTI FutureSafe for a conversation with Kimberly S. Budil, PhD, Director of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, on the nuclear security enterprise—and how we can tailor it for our future. 

As governments grapple with how to effectively harness the benefits and mitigate the risks of emerging technologies and AI, Budil will discuss the future of developing and maintaining the U.S. nuclear arsenal and enhancing national security through the military application of nuclear science. 

Budil is the 13th Director of the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL). She sets the strategic vision for LLNL and ensures the enhancement of national security through the application of cutting-edge science and technology. Along with the directors of Los Alamos and Sandia national laboratories, she shares the responsibility of providing the U.S. government with an annual institutional assessment of the safety, security, and effectiveness of U.S. nuclear weapons.

recentItems.title: Ghosts of Hiroshima: 80 Years at the Nuclear Brink
recentItems.description: Join CNN Anchor, Christiane Amanpour for a conversation with Academy Award-winning director James Cameron and Nuclear Threat Initiative CEO Ernest J. Moniz. The conversation will preview Ghosts of Hiroshima, a new book out this week to coincide with the 80th commemoration of the Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombings. This hour-long discussion will cover why Cameron and Moniz are sounding the alarm on the today’s nuclear threats and highlight the power of storytelling to imagine a safer future.

recentItems.title: NTI Seminar: A Conversation with New York Times Opinion
recentItems.description:
The latest addition in our NTI Seminar Series features a conversation with Kathleen Kingsbury and W.J. Hennigan from New York Times Opinion on their “At the Brink” series about today’s nuclear threats.

For the past year, Times Opinion has delivered essays, podcasts, and videos to bring the peril of nuclear weapons back to the forefront of public consciousness. The multi-part, interactive project immerses readers into today’s realities by explaining the deteriorating security environment, scrutinizing policies, and offering ways for nations — and its citizenry — to drive practical changes.

Kathleen Kingsbury is the Opinion Editor for The New York Times. In her role, she oversees the editorial board, guest essays, Opinion columnists, letters to the editor, as well as Opinion’s newsletters, audio, video, graphics, design and digital distribution teams. Prior to joining The Times in 2017, Kingsbury worked at the Boston Globe and Time magazine. In 2015, while at The Globe, Katie won a Pulitzer Prize for Editorial Writing for her series “Service Not Included.”

W.J. Hennigan writes about the U.S. military and national security issues for The New York Times Opinion section in Washington, D.C. He has covered war, the arms trade, and the lives of U.S. service members for more than 15 years. He’s worked for The Los Angeles Times and Time magazine, and has reported from more than two dozen countries, including Iraq, Afghanistan, and from the Horn of Africa.
